title: Question 2
stem:
An ideal gas is contained in a cylinder by means of a movable frictionless piston, as illustrated in Fig. 2.1.

{{figure:figure_2_1}}

Fig. 2.1

Initially, the gas has a volume of $1.8 \times 10^{-3} \text{m}^3$ at a pressure of $3.3 \times 10^5 \text{Pa}$ and a temperature of $310 \text{K}$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Show that the number of gas molecules in the cylinder is $1.4 \times 10^{23}$.
hints: Hint 1: Look at what you are given - pressure, volume and thermodynamic temperature - and think which ideal gas law connects these directly to the number of molecules N.
Hint 2: Rearrange that relation to make N the subject, then check you are using SI units for p in Pa, V in m^3 and T in K with k = 1.38 x 10^-23 J K^-1.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choose the molecular form of the ideal gas law**
For an ideal gas, pressure and volume are linked to temperature by the motion of N individual molecules. That link is $$pV = NkT$$ where $k$ is the Boltzmann constant $1.38 \times 10^{-23} \text{ J K}^{-1}$. This is the right form here because you want N, not moles n.

Step 2: **Rearrange and substitute to show N**
Make N the subject before putting numbers in: $$N = \frac{pV}{kT}$$ Then substitute $p = 3.3 \times 10^5 \text{ Pa}$, $V = 1.8 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}^3$, $T = 310 \text{ K}$: $$N = \frac{(3.3 \times 10^5)(1.8 \times 10^{-3})}{(1.38 \times 10^{-23})(310)} \approx 1.39 \times 10^{23} \approx 1.4 \times 10^{23}$$ This confirms the given value to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Use kinetic theory to explain why, when the piston is moved so that the gas expands, this causes a decrease in the temperature of the gas.

markscheme_points.text: speed of molecule decreases on impact with moving piston

mean square speed (directly) proportional to (thermodynamic) temperature or mean square speed (directly) proportional to kinetic energy (of molecules) or kinetic energy (of molecules) (directly) proportional to (thermodynamic temperature)
kinetic energy (of molecules) decreases (so temperature decreases)

hints: Hint 1: Picture a single molecule hitting the piston in Fig. 2.1 while the piston is moving outward - think about the rebound speed compared to the incident speed, like a ball hitting a bat moving away.
Hint 2: Recall how the average translational kinetic energy of molecules is linked to thermodynamic temperature for an ideal gas.
Hint 3: Connect the change in molecular speed on many collisions to the change in total kinetic energy and hence to temperature.
parts.proper_answer: Molecules rebound from the receding piston with reduced speed and hence reduced kinetic energy. Since mean molecular kinetic energy is proportional to thermodynamic temperature, the temperature falls.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What happens at the moving piston**
When the gas expands, the piston moves outward. A molecule hitting it rebounds elastically in the piston frame, but in the laboratory frame the wall is running away. So the reflected speed is less than the incident speed, just as a tennis ball loses speed when the racket moves back. Each collision therefore removes a little kinetic energy from the molecule.

Step 2: **Link kinetic energy to temperature**
Kinetic theory tells you that temperature is a measure of the average random translational kinetic energy: $$\frac{1}{2}m<c^2> = \frac{3}{2}kT$$ So $T$ is directly proportional to mean square speed $<c^2>$ and to mean kinetic energy. It is not about bulk motion, it is about random molecular motion.

Step 3: **Build the full cooling argument**
Many molecules strike the receding piston, so the average kinetic energy of the whole gas falls. Because average kinetic energy is proportional to $T$, the thermodynamic temperature must decrease. This is cooling by doing work with no heat input.

parts.label: (c)
(c)(i)
parts.text:
The average translational kinetic energy $E_{\text{K}}$ of a molecule of an ideal gas is given by
$$E_{\text{K}} = \frac{3}{2}kT$$
where $k$ is the Boltzmann constant and $T$ is the thermodynamic temperature.

Calculate the increase in internal energy $\Delta U$ of the gas during the expansion.
hints: Hint 1: Remember that for an ideal gas there is no potential energy, so internal energy is simply the sum of the average translational kinetic energies of all N molecules.
Hint 2: Write the change in total energy as N times the change in (3/2)kT, and work out the temperature change carefully with its sign from 310 K to 288 K.
Hint 3: Use N = 1.4 x 10^23 from (a) and k = 1.38 x 10^-23 J K^-1, and keep the negative sign to show a decrease.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Total internal energy from molecular energy**
An ideal gas has only kinetic energy, no intermolecular potential energy. So total internal energy $U$ is N times the mean energy per molecule: $$U = N E_K = N \left(\frac{3}{2}kT\right)$$ A change in $T$ therefore gives a change in $U$.

Step 2: **Form the change**
Subtract initial from final: $$\Delta U = \frac{3}{2}Nk\Delta T = \frac{3}{2}Nk(T_2 - T_1)$$ Here $T_1 = 310 \text{ K}$ and $T_2 = 288 \text{ K}$, so $$\Delta T = 288 - 310 = -22 \text{ K}$$ The negative sign already tells you internal energy will fall.

Step 3: **Calculate the value**
Insert $N = 1.4 \times 10^{23}$ and $k = 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \text{ J K}^{-1}$: $$\Delta U = 1.5 \times (1.4 \times 10^{23}) \times (1.38 \times 10^{-23}) \times (-22)$$ $$\Delta U \approx -64 \text{ J}$$ The increase is negative, meaning a decrease of about $64 \text{ J}$.

marking_points.text: $\Delta U = 3/2 \times k \times \Delta T \times N$

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text:
The work done by the gas during the expansion is $76 \text{J}$.

Use your answer in (i) to explain whether thermal energy is transferred to or from the gas during the expansion.

markscheme_points.text: decrease in internal energy is less than work done by gas
(thermal energy is) transferred to the gas (during the expansion)

hints: Hint 1: Compare the two energy numbers side by side - the gas does 76 J of work pushing the piston out, but its internal store only drops by about 64 J.
Hint 2: Use energy conservation from the first law to decide whether the missing energy must have come into the gas as heat or left the gas as heat.
parts.proper_answer: The decrease in internal energy, 64 J, is less than the 76 J of work done by the gas. By the first law, extra energy must be supplied, so thermal energy is transferred to the gas during the expansion.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Compare work and internal energy change**
The gas does $W = 76 \text{ J}$ of work on the piston. If the expansion were adiabatic, that work would come entirely from internal energy and $\Delta U$ would be $-76 \text{ J}$. In fact $\Delta U$ is only about $-64 \text{ J}$. The internal drop is smaller in magnitude than the work done.

Step 2: **Apply the first law to find heat flow**
The first law is $$\Delta U = q + W_{on}$$ where $W_{on} = -76 \text{ J}$ for work done by the gas. So $$-64 = q - 76$$ giving $q \approx +12 \text{ J}$. A positive $q$ means net thermal energy is transferred to the gas from the surroundings during the expansion to make up the shortfall.
